title: Attacking Shape Foundations
primarySkill: Establishing an effective attacking shape around the football.
objective: Develop players’ understanding of how to form and maintain a balanced attacking shape that provides forward, lateral and release options for the player in possession.
groundSize: A rectangular area approximately 40 metres long by 30 metres wide, divided into three horizontal zones.
equipment: Three marker poles or cone gates
setup:
Divide players into two attacking groups of equal size.
One group operates at a time while the other group observes or completes a separate ball-handling activity.
Place one starting player with the football at one end of the area.
Position three to five teammates ahead of the football across the width and depth of the area.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
No defenders are used initially.
Players must avoid standing in a straight horizontal or vertical line.
howTheDrillWorks:
The starting player begins with the football and scans the attacking shape ahead.
Teammates establish at least one forward option, one lateral option and one release option behind or beside the football.
The football is moved by kick or handball through the area while all players adjust their positions after every disposal.
The player who disposes must immediately move to create another support option rather than remaining stationary.
The group scores by carrying or disposing the football through the scoring gate without two attackers occupying the same running lane.
Players reset at the opposite end and repeat in the other direction.
After several repetitions, introduce a five-second limit for the player in possession.
Rotate the observing group into the activity.
coachingPoints: Create options in front of, beside and behind the player in possession.
Avoid forming a flat line across the ground.
Maintain enough separation for each player to remain a genuine disposal option.
Adjust immediately when the football changes position.
Communicate early using names, direction and available space.
The nearest player should provide quick support without crowding the ball carrier.
Players further from the football should maintain width and depth.
Continue moving after disposing of the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players establish multiple disposal angles before the ball carrier comes under pressure.
Whether players maintain width and depth rather than following the football.
Whether the disposer moves again after releasing the football.
Whether players communicate before the football arrives.
Whether the attacking shape adjusts as possession moves through each zone.
Whether players can identify when the shape has become too flat or congested.
progressions: Add one passive defender who applies shadow pressure to the player in possession.
Add a second defender who attempts to close the most obvious passing lane.
Require the group to use both sides of the area before scoring.
Introduce a turnover consequence if two attackers occupy the same lane.
Allow defenders to become fully active once the attacking shape is consistently maintained.
regressions: Use handball only over a smaller area.
Mark fixed starting positions for forward, lateral and release options.
Pause after each disposal and allow the coach to reposition players.
successIndicators: Provide at least three different disposal angles.
Move immediately after disposing of the football.
Reach the scoring gate without the shape collapsing around the ball carrier.
matchApplication: The drill introduces the basic attacking structure required whenever a team wins possession. Effective teams provide the ball carrier with options ahead of the football, across the ground and behind the contest. Maintaining this shape reduces congestion, improves possession retention and allows the team to move the football towards goal without relying on a single predictable option.
relatedDrills: DM-100 – Decision Making Chapter Final Assessment

title: Width Before Speed
primarySkill: Using width to open attacking space before accelerating ball movement.
objective: Teach players to establish and use attacking width before attempting to move the football quickly through congested central areas.
groundSize: A 50-metre-long by 40-metre-wide area divided into a central corridor and two outside lanes.
setup:
Mark a central lane approximately 15 metres wide.
Mark two outside lanes, each approximately 12 metres wide.
Divide players into an attacking team and a smaller defending team.
Use a six-versus-three or eight-versus-four format.
Position the attacking team throughout all three lanes.
Start the football at one end of the central lane.
Place a scoring gate at the opposite end.
Defenders begin inside the central lane and may move into an outside lane only after the football enters it.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins in possession at one end.
Before progressing through the middle third of the area, the attackers must complete at least one disposal into an outside lane.
Wide players must remain available near the boundary-side cones without standing still.
Once the football reaches an outside lane, central attackers reposition to create forward and inside-return options.
The team may then continue down the outside or transfer the football back through the centre.
Defenders attempt to delay play, close central lanes and force rushed disposals.
The attacking team scores by moving the football through the far scoring gate.
A turnover occurs if the football is intercepted, leaves the area or is held for longer than five seconds.
Teams reset and rotate defenders after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Establish width before attempting to attack at maximum speed.
Wide players should stay outside the immediate congestion.
The ball carrier must scan both sides before selecting an option.
Players inside the ground should not drift towards the wide receiver too early.
Use width to stretch defenders and create space inside.
Accelerate once the defensive shape has been moved.
Support the wide receiver with an option ahead and an option back inside.
Avoid slow sideways movement that does not alter the defensive structure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether wide players establish position before the ball carrier needs them.
Whether the attacking team uses width with purpose rather than simply moving sideways.
Whether central players maintain their spacing when the football travels outside.
Whether the wide receiver has forward and inside support.
Whether the team accelerates after shifting the defenders.
Whether players recognise when the corridor becomes available.
progressions: Allow defenders to enter outside lanes immediately.
Require a switch from one outside lane to the other before scoring.
Introduce an end-zone target who must mark the final disposal.
Add a scoring bonus for returning through the corridor after using width.
Play continuously after turnovers so teams must transition immediately.
regressions: Increase the width of the outside lanes.
Require only handball over a shorter distance.
Place fixed receivers in each outside lane.
successIndicators: Establish width before the football arrives.
Use the outside lane to alter the defensive shape.
Maintain central support rather than following the football.
Identify and use the corridor when it becomes available.
matchApplication: Teams often lose possession when they attack directly into a crowded corridor without first moving the opposition. Effective width forces defenders to spread, creates uncontested possession and can open central attacking lanes. The drill teaches players that width is not passive possession; it is a method of creating space for faster and more dangerous ball movement.

title: Depth and Staggered Support
primarySkill: Creating attacking depth through staggered support positions.
objective: Develop players’ ability to create staggered attacking options at different depths so the ball carrier can move forward, laterally or backwards without the team becoming flat.
groundSize: A rectangular area 50 metres long by 30 metres wide, divided into five depth bands.
setup:
Mark five horizontal bands across the length of the area.
Position one or two attackers in each band.
Start the football with a player in the first band.
Players may move between bands once the drill begins.
No more than two attackers may occupy the same band at one time.
Use one passive defender initially.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
howTheDrillWorks:
The starting player receives the football and scans ahead.
The closest forward player leads into the next available band.
A second player provides a deeper option beyond the first lead.
Another attacker maintains a support position behind or level with the football.
After each disposal, the players rotate through the depth bands.
The player who receives must have at least two options at different depths before disposing.
The passive defender closes one option but does not intercept during early repetitions.
The group moves the football through all five bands and scores through the end gate.
Once the sequence is completed, players reset and begin from the opposite end.
Increase defensive pressure as the group becomes more organised.
coachingPoints: Avoid placing all attacking options at the same depth.
The first lead should create space for a deeper lead.
Maintain a player behind the football as a release option.
Lead at an angle rather than directly at the ball carrier.
Time movement so the next option appears as the football is received.
Rotate positions after disposal rather than returning to the same cone.
Communicate which option is short, deep or behind.
Preserve space between consecutive leads.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players provide options at genuinely different depths.
Whether the first lead clears space for a second option.
Whether the release player remains available behind the football.
Whether players rotate after disposing.
Whether the ball carrier scans beyond the closest option.
Whether players maintain adequate separation between depth bands.
progressions: Reduce the maximum number of attackers allowed in each band to one.
Award two points for using the deepest safe option.
Allow immediate transition if defenders win possession.
regressions: Allow players to hold fixed positions.
Pause after each disposal to rebuild the shape.
Increase the width of the area.
successIndicators: Provide short, intermediate and deep options.
Maintain a release player behind the football.
Lead without crowding another player’s space.
Rotate into new positions after disposal.
Progress the football without the attacking shape becoming flat.
matchApplication: Attacking teams need depth to move through defensive lines. When all players stand level with each other, the ball carrier has limited disposal angles and defenders can cover several options at once. Staggered support creates layered options, protects possession and allows the team to continue attacking even when the first forward option is denied.

title: Five-Metre Spacing Grid
primarySkill: Maintaining functional spacing between attacking players.
objective: Teach players to recognise and maintain sufficient spacing so each attacker remains a usable option without creating excessive gaps between teammates.
groundSize: A 35-metre by 35-metre square divided into nine equal grid sections.
setup:
Create a three-by-three grid using cones.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with six attackers against two defenders.
No more than two attackers may occupy one grid section.
Attackers should begin spread across the grid.
One football is used.
Defenders may move freely throughout the entire area.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team maintains possession by handball or short kick.
After disposing, a player must move into a different grid section.
Attackers may not stand closer than approximately five metres from a teammate unless completing a brief overlap.
Defenders attempt to intercept or force the football outside the area.
The attackers score one point for every six consecutive disposals.
A bonus point is awarded if possession uses all three columns of the grid during the sequence.
If two attackers remain crowded in the same section for longer than three seconds, possession transfers to the defenders.
Rotate defenders every 60–90 seconds.
Continue for several rounds and challenge the group to improve its highest possession score.
coachingPoints: Maintain enough space to remain a separate option.
Do not move automatically towards the player in possession.
Replace space vacated by a teammate.
Scan before moving so two players do not enter the same area.
Move after disposal to improve the team’s shape.
Use short, sharp movements rather than constant slow drifting.
The closest support player should be available without blocking another option.
Spread quickly after congestion forms.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise when the area around the football is becoming congested.
Whether disposers move into new space.
Whether players spread across the full width of the grid.
Whether attackers maintain connection without standing too close.
Whether players communicate before entering an occupied section.
Whether the ball carrier has more than one clear disposal option.
progressions: Require at least one kick during every six-disposal sequence.
Introduce immediate transition to a small scoring gate after a turnover.
regressions: Allow attackers to remain in the same section after disposal.
Pause play to identify open and crowded areas.
successIndicators: Move into available sections after disposal.
Use the entire width of the grid.
Support the ball carrier without crowding.
Complete possession sequences with several clear disposal options available.
matchApplication: Players often reduce their own team’s attacking options by gathering around the football. Functional spacing forces defenders to cover more ground, gives the ball carrier clearer disposal lanes and creates room for teammates to accelerate. The drill develops awareness of when to support closely and when to remain away from the immediate contest.

title: Possession Support Triangle
primarySkill: Creating a three-player support triangle around the football.
objective: Develop a repeatable support pattern in which the player in possession has an option ahead, an option to the side and an option behind the football.
groundSize: A 45-metre-long by 30-metre-wide area with three cone gates positioned at each end.
setup:
Divide players into groups of three.
Each group begins with one football.
Position the first player with the football, the second player ahead and at an angle, and the third player behind or beside the football.
Set several lanes so multiple groups can operate simultaneously.
Add one passive defender per group after introductory repetitions.
Place a target gate at the far end of each lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins by moving forward.
The forward support player leads at an angle to create a disposal option.
The third player remains behind or laterally positioned as a release option.
The ball carrier disposes to either support player.
Immediately after disposing, the original ball carrier runs to become the next forward or lateral option.
The three players continuously rotate their positions while progressing down the lane.
The group must maintain a triangular shape rather than running in a straight line.
A passive defender closes one side of the triangle, forcing the ball carrier to use the alternative option.
The group scores by carrying or disposing through the end gate.
Players return through another lane and repeat.
coachingPoints: Keep the triangle wide enough to create separate disposal lanes.
The forward player should lead at an angle.
The release player must remain behind the line of the football.
The disposer must move immediately to rebuild the triangle.
Communicate which side is available.
Avoid running directly behind another player.
Use the release option when forward movement is blocked.
Accelerate after the football is released.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the triangle is maintained while the group moves.
Whether the disposer immediately becomes another option.
Whether the release player stays behind or beside the football.
Whether players use angled rather than straight-line running.
Whether the ball carrier scans both support options.
Whether the group changes direction when the defender blocks one side.
progressions: Allow groups to move freely through a larger shared area.
Require one switch of direction before scoring.
Continue immediately into a four-versus-two possession game.
regressions: Pause after each disposal to rebuild the triangle.
successIndicators: Select the option not covered by the defender.
matchApplication: A three-player support triangle is a common attacking pattern around contests, stoppages and open play. It allows the team to continue forward when possible while retaining a safe release option if pressure closes the direct route. Players who understand the pattern can support possession without crowding the football.

title: Ball-Side and Weak-Side Balance
primarySkill: Balancing attacking support between the ball side and weak side of the ground.
objective: Teach players to support the immediate ball movement while preserving weak-side options that can be used when the opposition compresses towards the football.
groundSize: Half-ground width or a rectangular area approximately 60 metres long by 50 metres wide, divided into left, central and right channels.
setup:
Mark three vertical channels: left, centre and right.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Use eight attackers against four defenders initially.
Position approximately two-thirds of the attackers on or near the starting ball side.
Position the remaining attackers in weak-side roles.
Begin the football near one boundary.
Set a scoring gate at the opposite end.
Defenders may move freely but should initially compress towards the ball side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession near one outside channel.
Ball-side players provide immediate short and forward support.
Weak-side players hold width and depth rather than crossing towards the football.
The attacking team may progress down the ball side or transfer possession through the central channel.
If defenders compress and deny forward movement, the attackers attempt to switch to the weak side.
A switch scores one bonus point if the weak-side receiver takes possession in space.
The team scores a further point by moving the football through the end gate.
Defenders score by intercepting or forcing the football outside the area.
After each repetition, restart from the opposite side so players practise both roles.
Rotate attackers and defenders after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Ball-side players should provide immediate connection.
Weak-side players must remain patient and preserve space.
Do not bring every attacker to the football.
Scan across the ground before possession is received.
Use the central channel to connect a switch.
Weak-side players should adjust their depth as the football moves.
Switch quickly once the defence has compressed.
Communicate early when the far side becomes available.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether weak-side players maintain width.
Whether ball-side support remains connected without crowding.
Whether players scan before receiving.
Whether the attacking team recognises defensive compression.
Whether the switch occurs early enough to exploit space.
Whether weak-side players adjust their depth rather than standing still.
progressions: Allow defenders to begin in a balanced shape rather than pre-compressing.
Require the attacking team to identify whether to continue ball side or switch.
Award two points for a switch that leads directly to a forward entry.
regressions: Freeze weak-side players in starting zones.
Use a coach call to signal when the switch is available.
Allow uncontested marks during the first phase.
successIndicators: Maintain both ball-side connection and weak-side width.
Avoid pulling every attacker towards the football.
Transfer possession through a safe connecting option.
Receive on the weak side with space to continue attacking.
matchApplication: When the opposition shifts heavily towards the football, space develops on the opposite side of the ground. Teams that preserve weak-side structure can switch into this space and attack against a moving defence. The drill teaches players that those away from the football remain critical to the attacking phase.

title: Corridor Window Access
primarySkill: Identifying and using safe opportunities to access the corridor.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when the corridor is open, create a safe central option and use it without forcing possession into congestion.
groundSize: A rectangular area 60 metres long by 45 metres wide with a 15-metre central corridor and two outside lanes.
setup:
Mark a central corridor from one end to the other.
Divide the remaining space into two outside lanes.
Use seven attackers against four defenders.
Begin the football in an outside lane.
Position one or two attacking players in staggered central roles.
Defenders begin between the football and the corridor.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
The corridor may be entered only through a controlled disposal to a moving receiver.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in an outside lane.
Attackers move the football while central players adjust their depth and leading angle.
Defenders attempt to protect the corridor and delay forward movement.
The ball carrier must decide whether the central option is safe.
If the corridor is closed, possession remains outside and the team continues to shift the defence.
If a central window opens, an attacker leads into the space and calls early.
The football is delivered to the central receiver, who turns and moves forward immediately.
The attacking team scores two points for using the corridor and exiting through the scoring gate.
It scores one point for reaching the gate through an outside lane.
A forced or intercepted corridor disposal gives the defenders two points.
Rotate roles after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Access the corridor only when the receiver has separation and a clear exit.
Central players should lead into space rather than standing in the corridor.
The ball carrier must scan before receiving.
Shift defenders laterally before attempting the central disposal.
Deliver the football to the receiver’s advantage.
The central receiver should turn forward where possible.
Support must arrive ahead and behind the central possession.
Avoid treating the corridor as compulsory.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier scans the corridor before receiving.
Whether central leads are timed after defenders shift.
Whether players force central disposals into occupied space.
Whether the central receiver has an immediate next option.
Whether the attacking team supports ahead and behind.
Whether outside possession remains purposeful when the corridor is closed.
progressions: Reduce the width of the corridor.
Require a corridor entry to be followed by a forward kick.
Play continuously after turnovers with the defending team attacking the opposite direction.
regressions: Allow the coach to call when the corridor is open.
Position a fixed target inside the corridor.
successIndicators: Move defenders before attempting central access.
Time central leads into available space.
Continue attacking quickly after a successful corridor entry.
matchApplication: The corridor provides the shortest route to goal but carries greater turnover risk. Effective teams create and identify safe central windows rather than entering blindly. This drill develops the judgement required to balance attacking reward with possession security.

title: Coordinated Forward Leading Lanes
primarySkill: Coordinating multiple forward leads without crowding the same space.
objective: Teach forwards to coordinate short, deep and clearing leads so the ball carrier receives distinct forward-entry options rather than several players leading into the same lane.
groundSize: An area from approximately 70 metres from goal to the goal square, using the full width of the forward 50 where available.
setup:
Position three forwards inside the attacking area.
Assign one as the short lead, one as the deep lead and one as the clearing or opposite-side lead.
Position two or three attackers outside the forward 50 as the entry group.
Add two defenders initially.
Mark three leading lanes using cones.
Begin the football approximately 60–70 metres from goal.
Use a goalkeeper or spare player to return footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The entry group moves the football until one player is in position to deliver inside 50.
The short forward leads towards the ball carrier.
The deep forward delays, then leads into the space created behind the short lead.
The third forward clears laterally or leads to the opposite side.
Defenders attempt to track the leads and protect dangerous space.
The ball carrier selects the best available option rather than automatically using the first lead.
The selected forward attempts to mark and complete a set shot or quick scoring action.
Unselected forwards continue moving to create crumbing and secondary options.
Players reset with different forwards assigned to each role.
Increase defender freedom as the timing and spacing improve.
coachingPoints: Only one forward should attack each leading lane.
The first lead must create space for the second.
Deep leads should be delayed until the defender reacts.
Clearing leads must be purposeful and remove defenders from the target area.
The ball carrier should scan all options before entering.
Deliver the football to the forward’s advantage.
Unused forwards must remain involved after the entry.
Communicate leading roles before the attacking phase begins.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether forwards enter separate lanes.
Whether the deep lead is delayed appropriately.
Whether the clearing forward moves a defender away.
Whether the ball carrier scans beyond the first option.
Whether the football is delivered to the receiver’s advantage.
Whether forwards react after the initial entry.
progressions: Allow forwards to choose and communicate roles live.
Begin from a turnover or stoppage simulation.
Continue play until a score or defensive exit occurs.
regressions: Have the coach call the lead sequence.
Use one short and one deep forward only.
successIndicators: Time short and deep movements effectively.
Provide the ball carrier with distinct options.
Continue working after the initial forward entry.
matchApplication: Forward entries often break down when several forwards lead towards the same football. Coordinated leading patterns stretch defenders, protect dangerous space and improve the quality of the entry. The drill develops the communication and timing needed for a functioning forward structure.

title: Line-to-Line Connection Chain
primarySkill: Connecting defenders, midfielders and forwards during attacking ball movement.
objective: Develop coordinated movement between the defensive, midfield and forward lines so the football can progress without large gaps or disconnected attacking phases.
groundSize: Three-quarter ground or full ground, divided into defensive, midfield and forward zones.
setup:
Divide the ground into three horizontal zones.
Assign attackers to defensive, midfield and forward-line groups.
Use approximately 12 attackers against six defenders.
Begin the football in the defensive zone.
At least two attackers must start in each zone.
Players may move between zones after the football is disposed.
Defenders begin with two players in each zone.
Use the main goals or a scoring gate at the attacking end.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession in the defensive zone.
Defensive players create width and identify a connection into the midfield zone.
Midfielders provide one option towards the football and one option ahead.
Once possession enters the midfield zone, a defensive player pushes forward to maintain connection behind the football.
Forwards coordinate their leading patterns as the midfield possession is secured.
The attacking team attempts to enter the forward zone and score.
Players may not skip an entire zone with the first disposal during early repetitions.
Defenders apply pressure and attempt to intercept.
If the defenders win possession, they score by carrying the football back through the starting gate.
After each repetition, rotate players between the three line groups.
coachingPoints: Keep each line connected to the next.
Avoid leaving the player in possession isolated between zones.
Midfielders should provide both a short connection and a forward option.
Defenders must advance after releasing the football.
Forwards should begin their leads as midfield possession is secured.
Maintain width across all three lines.
Communicate the next option before the football arrives.
React immediately if possession is lost.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether gaps form between the three playing lines.
Whether defensive players advance after disposal.
Whether midfielders connect behind and ahead of the football.
Whether forwards time their movement with midfield possession.
Whether the team maintains width while progressing.
Whether players react collectively after turnovers.
progressions: Remove the rule requiring possession through each zone.
Begin from a contested ground ball or stoppage.
Require the team to use both sides of the ground during the possession chain.
regressions: Fix two connection players in each zone.
Pause when possession enters a new zone.
Allow uncontested marks during the first phase.
successIndicators: Maintain connection between all three lines.
Provide support behind and ahead of the football.
Time forward leads with midfield control.
Enter the forward line without isolated or rushed possession.
matchApplication: Successful team offence requires the entire side to move as one connected unit. When defenders, midfielders and forwards become separated, the ball carrier is forced into low-percentage disposals. This drill develops the coordinated movement required to move possession from the back half into a scoring opportunity.

title: Scoring Method Choice Game
primarySkill: Selecting the most appropriate scoring method from an attacking possession.
objective: Develop players’ ability to assess defensive positioning and choose between a direct shot, a lead-up mark, a running score, a short pass or continued possession.
groundSize: Approximately 70 metres from goal using the full width of the forward half.
setup:
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Use eight attackers against six defenders.
Position the football approximately 60–70 metres from goal.
Start with attackers in a balanced shape across the width and depth of the area.
Place two defenders inside the forward 50, two across the high-forward area and two near the starting possession.
Use the main goals.
Prepare a scoring system that rewards different attacking outcomes.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with controlled possession outside the forward 50.
Defenders organise in one of several shapes selected by the coach.
Attackers must scan the defensive shape before beginning the forward movement.
The team may attempt a direct shot, deliver to a leading forward, use a running handball chain, pass short to improve the angle or retain possession and reset.
A goal scores six points.
A behind scores one point.
A marked forward entry that produces a set shot scores one bonus point.
A running score created through an overlap scores one bonus point.
A turnover caused by a forced or low-percentage attacking decision gives the defenders two points.
If no safe scoring option is available, the attackers may recycle possession outside the forward 50 without penalty.
After a score or turnover, reset with a different defensive shape.
Rotate attackers and defenders after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Scan the defensive structure before choosing the scoring method.
Do not treat every possession as an automatic kick inside 50.
Use a leading target when the forward has separation.
Use a running score when defenders are drawn towards the ball carrier.
Retain possession when the forward area is outnumbered.
Improve the angle when a short option is available.
Forwards should provide aerial, ground-level and space-clearing options.
The decision should match the position of teammates and defenders.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan before entering the forward area.
Whether the chosen scoring method suits the defensive shape.
Whether attackers recognise outnumbered situations.
Whether forwards provide different types of options.
Whether players retain possession instead of forcing an entry.
Whether the team reacts to missed marks and ground-level football.
Whether decisions improve across repeated scenarios.
progressions: Allow defenders to transition to goals at the opposite end after turnovers.
Increase defender numbers to create temporary outnumbered forward situations.
Remove the coach-selected defensive shape and allow defenders to organise independently.
regressions: Call out the available scoring method during early repetitions.
Limit the activity to two scoring choices before expanding the decision set.
successIndicators: Assess the defensive shape before attacking.
Select a scoring method suited to the available space.
Retain possession when no safe scoring option exists.
Adapt their decisions when the defensive structure changes.
matchApplication: Attacking teams must create scores in different ways. Some situations require a direct shot, while others demand a lead-up mark, overlap run, short pass, ground-level contest or possession reset. This drill introduces players to the tactical decision that scoring efficiency depends not only on execution, but also on selecting the correct method for the situation.

title: Release Runner Recognition
primarySkill: Identifying and using a release runner outside congestion.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise pressure around the football and release possession to a teammate moving into clear attacking space.
groundSize: A 35-metre-long by 25-metre-wide area with a central congestion zone and two outside release lanes.
setup:
Mark a central square approximately 12 metres by 12 metres.
Mark one release lane on each side of the square.
Place three attackers and two defenders inside the central square.
Position one attacking release runner in each outside lane.
Place a scoring gate 15–20 metres beyond the congestion zone.
Begin each repetition with a ground ball or handball fed into the central square.
Rotate release runners, inside attackers and defenders regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach feeds the football into the central congestion zone.
Inside attackers compete to secure possession while defenders apply controlled pressure.
Once possession is won, the ball carrier scans for a release runner in either outside lane.
Release runners time their movement so they arrive outside the congestion as possession is secured.
The ball carrier handballs or kicks to the available release runner.
The release runner accelerates towards the scoring gate.
Inside attackers exit the congestion and provide forward or lateral support.
Defenders may chase once the release disposal is made.
The attacking group scores by carrying or disposing the football through the gate.
A turnover occurs if the release disposal is intercepted, missed or directed back into congestion.
Reset with a new feed and rotate roles after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Scan outside the congestion before taking possession where possible.
Release runners should begin away from the football and arrive late.
Present on an angle rather than directly behind the ball carrier.
The ball carrier should protect the football before releasing.
Handball to the runner’s path rather than directly at the body.
Accelerate immediately after receiving outside.
Inside players must follow the release and reconnect.
Use communication early enough to influence the ball carrier’s decision.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan outside the contest before possession is secured.
Whether release runners remain clear of congestion.
Whether runners time their movement rather than waiting stationary.
Whether the ball carrier protects possession before releasing.
Whether the disposal allows the receiver to continue moving.
Whether inside attackers reconnect after the initial release.
progressions: Add an additional defender inside the congestion.
Allow one defender to track a release runner.
Require the release runner to choose between continuing forward and switching across the ground.
regressions: Use a clean handball feed rather than a ground ball.
Fix the release runner on one side only.
Allow the coach to call the open lane.
successIndicators: Maintain a clear release option outside.
Deliver the football to the runner’s advantage.
Convert the release into forward movement.
matchApplication: Contested possession often becomes valuable only when it is released to a player outside the immediate pressure. The drill teaches inside players to find that option and outside players to remain disciplined enough to receive in space.

title: Switch Through the Back
primarySkill: Transferring possession safely through players positioned behind the football.
objective: Teach players to use supporting teammates behind the football to escape pressure and transfer possession to the open side of the ground.
groundSize: A 55-metre-long by 50-metre-wide area divided into left, central and right channels.
setup:
Mark three vertical channels across the area.
Use eight attackers against four defenders.
Begin the football in one outside channel.
Position two attacking support players behind the football across the central and opposite channels.
Place two forward targets further ahead.
Defenders begin compressed towards the starting side.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
The attacking team may not kick directly across the full width during the introductory phase.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession near one side.
Defenders apply pressure and close the forward lane.
The ball carrier uses a safe disposal to a supporting player behind the football.
The support player scans across the ground before receiving.
Possession is transferred through one or more supporting players towards the open side.
Wide attackers on the far side hold their position until the switch begins.
Once the football reaches the open side, the team accelerates forward.
Attackers score by moving through the far scoring gate.
Defenders score by intercepting or forcing the football outside the area.
Reset from the opposite side and rotate support roles after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Maintain support behind the football before pressure arrives.
The first release disposal must be safe and controlled.
Supporting players should receive facing the field where possible.
Transfer through connected options rather than attempting a risky long switch.
Far-side players must hold width and avoid drifting towards the ball.
Accelerate after the defensive shape has shifted.
Communicate the switch before the first release disposal.
The original ball carrier should move again after releasing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether support exists behind the football before pressure develops.
Whether receivers scan before possession arrives.
Whether the switch is completed through safe disposal angles.
Whether far-side players maintain width.
Whether the attacking team increases speed after reaching the open side.
Whether the first ball carrier reconnects after the release.
progressions: Allow defenders to spread rather than pre-compress.
Remove the requirement to switch and allow players to decide whether to continue down the original side.
Add one defender behind the football.
Permit long switches when the option is genuinely safe.
regressions: Place fixed supporting players behind the football.
successIndicators: Transfer the football without exposing the team to unnecessary risk.
Recognise when the switch has created an attacking advantage.
matchApplication: Teams often become trapped near the boundary when every player moves ahead of the football. Support behind possession allows the team to escape pressure, change the point of attack and access space on the opposite side.

title: Numbers at the Contest Exit
primarySkill: Creating a numerical advantage immediately outside a contest.
objective: Develop players’ ability to position multiple attacking options around a contest so possession can be released quickly and cleanly into space.
groundSize: A 45-metre-long by 35-metre-wide area with a central contest circle and an attacking end zone.
setup:
Mark a central contest circle approximately 10 metres in diameter.
Place two attackers and two defenders inside the circle.
Position three attacking support players and two defensive support players outside the circle.
Mark a scoring gate 20 metres ahead of the contest.
Begin each repetition with a ball-up, throw-in simulation or ground-ball feed.
Outside support players may not enter the circle until possession is clearly won.
howTheDrillWorks:
Inside players compete for possession.
Outside attackers position themselves on different angles around the contest.
Once an attacker wins possession, the nearest safe support option presents.
The second and third support players maintain separation and prepare for the next disposal.
The football is released outside by handball or short kick.
Attackers attempt to create a three-versus-two advantage moving towards the scoring gate.
Defenders chase, pressure and attempt to force a turnover.
The attacking team scores by carrying or disposing through the gate.
Defenders score if they intercept or lock the football inside the contest for five seconds.
Rotate inside and outside roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Outside attackers should position on different angles.
Avoid placing all support on the same side of the contest.
The nearest support player must remain visible to the ball winner.
Secondary support should anticipate the next disposal.
Release possession before pressure closes.
Use numerical advantage to move the football rather than invite contact.
Outside players must remain active without entering congestion early.
Communicate who is supporting short and who is holding wider.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attacking support is balanced around the contest.
Whether outside players stay clear until possession is won.
Whether the ball winner identifies the nearest safe release.
Whether secondary support anticipates the next action.
Whether attackers use the numerical advantage quickly.
Whether support players remain separated under pressure.
progressions: Add another defender outside the contest.
Allow support players to change positions before possession is won.
Remove the scoring gate and play to a leading target.
Continue live in both directions after turnovers.
regressions: Use passive contact inside the circle.
Increase the distance between the contest and defenders.
Pause after possession is won to identify support positions.
successIndicators: Create multiple options outside the contest.
Use the numerical advantage to gain territory.
Connect the first and second disposals after the contest.
matchApplication: Winning the football at a contest is only the first part of attacking play. Teams must position players outside the congestion so the possession can be converted into forward movement before defenders recover.

title: Overlap and Run-Past Timing
primarySkill: Timing an overlap run past the player in possession.
objective: Teach players to time a run past the ball carrier so the overlap creates forward momentum without crowding possession or attracting an extra defender too early.
groundSize: Several lanes approximately 35 metres long by 10 metres wide.
setup:
Divide players into groups of three or four.
Position one ball carrier at the start of each lane.
Place one support runner behind and slightly outside.
Position one defender five metres ahead.
Place a target gate at the end of the lane.
Use multiple lanes to minimise waiting.
The defender begins with controlled pressure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier moves towards the defender.
The support runner begins behind the ball carrier.
The ball carrier draws the defender while protecting the football.
The support runner accelerates past on the outside shoulder.
The ball carrier handballs into the runner’s path.
The overlap runner continues towards the gate.
The original ball carrier follows and becomes a support option.
The defender may chase after the handball is released.
The group scores by carrying or disposing through the gate.
Players rotate through ball carrier, runner and defender roles.
coachingPoints: The overlap runner should begin behind the football.
Accelerate late rather than arriving beside the ball carrier too early.
The ball carrier must draw the defender before releasing.
Run past the outside shoulder to remain visible.
Deliver the handball in front of the runner.
Continue supporting after the release.
Communicate the run without causing the defender to react too early.
Maintain enough width to avoid colliding with the ball carrier.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the runner begins behind the football.
Whether the ball carrier draws the defender.
Whether the runner arrives too early or too late.
Whether the handball allows continued acceleration.
Whether the original ball carrier reconnects.
Whether the overlap creates genuine forward momentum.
progressions: Add a second defender near the scoring gate.
Allow the ball carrier to choose whether to use the overlap.
Add a kick to a leading target after the overlap.
Run the activity in a larger shared space with multiple groups.
regressions: Use a fixed marker as the release point.
Allow the runner to call loudly before accelerating.
successIndicators: Begin the overlap from behind possession.
matchApplication: Overlap running allows a team to maintain speed and break a defensive line. Poorly timed overlap runs can crowd the ball carrier, attract defenders and reduce space. The drill develops the timing required to make the run an attacking advantage.

title: Fast or Control Tempo Game
primarySkill: Selecting the appropriate attacking tempo.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when to attack quickly and when to slow possession to rebuild attacking shape.
groundSize: A 55-metre-long by 40-metre-wide area divided into three horizontal zones.
setup:
Use eight attackers against five defenders.
Position players throughout the three zones.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
The coach holds two cue cards: one representing fast attack and one representing controlled possession.
Begin with the football in the first zone.
Defenders start in varied positions to create different attacking pictures.
The cue may be shown before or immediately after possession begins.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession in the first zone.
When the fast cue is shown, attackers must accelerate, run forward and attempt to score within ten seconds.
When the control cue is shown, attackers must retain possession and complete at least four disposals before entering the final zone.
The coach may change the cue during the possession.
Players must reorganise their movement and support according to the new tempo.
Defenders attempt to intercept or force the football outside the area.
Attackers score by moving through the gate under the correct tempo condition.
A turnover or failure to adjust to the cue gives defenders one point.
After several repetitions, remove the cue and allow players to choose the tempo based on defender positioning.
Rotate defenders after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Scan the numbers and space ahead before selecting tempo.
Fast attack requires direct running and support ahead of the football.
Controlled possession requires width, depth and safe options.
Do not confuse fast play with rushed disposal.
Slow possession should still move the defence.
Communicate tempo clearly across the group.
Be prepared to change tempo as the defensive picture changes.
Maintain support behind the football in both modes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise the current tempo requirement.
Whether movement patterns change appropriately.
Whether fast attack remains composed.
Whether controlled possession remains purposeful.
Whether communication reaches players away from the football.
Whether the team can change tempo during the same possession.
progressions: Allow defenders to change their structure during play.
regressions: Show the cue well before the repetition begins.
Use separate rounds for fast and controlled play.
successIndicators: Distinguish between opportunities for fast attack and possession control.
Adjust support movement to the selected tempo.
Rebuild shape when immediate attack is unavailable.
matchApplication: Teams cannot attack at one speed throughout a match. Some situations demand immediate movement before defenders recover, while others require patience and ball retention. The drill builds the shared recognition needed to control attacking tempo.

title: Inside-Out Attacking Movement
primarySkill: Moving possession from congestion to width before re-entering dangerous central space.
objective: Teach players to move the football outside congestion, stretch the defence and then identify an opportunity to attack back through the centre.
groundSize: A 60-metre-long by 50-metre-wide area with a central congestion zone, two outside lanes and a forward corridor gate.
setup:
Mark a 15-metre central congestion zone near the starting end.
Mark two outside lanes along the length of the area.
Place a corridor scoring gate near the attacking end.
Use nine attackers against six defenders.
Begin with three attackers and three defenders around the central contest.
Position remaining players in outside and forward support roles.
Start each repetition with a contested feed inside the central zone.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players contest the football in the central starting zone.
Once possession is won, attackers attempt to release outside.
Wide players provide movement ahead and beside the football.
The attacking team must complete at least one disposal in an outside lane.
Defenders shift towards the ball side.
Attackers then assess whether the corridor gate has opened.
If open, possession is transferred back inside to a moving receiver.
If closed, the team continues down the outside or switches play.
Two points are awarded for exiting congestion, using width and then scoring through the corridor gate.
One point is awarded for progressing through an outside gate.
Defenders score two points for intercepting a forced inside disposal.
Rotate contest and outside roles regularly.
coachingPoints: Escape the immediate pressure before attempting an aggressive inside disposal.
Wide players must establish position early.
Use outside possession to move defenders, not merely to satisfy a rule.
Central receivers should lead into the corridor rather than wait there.
Scan inside before receiving wide possession.
Re-enter only when the receiver has separation and a forward exit.
Maintain support behind the central receiver.
Continue outside if the corridor remains closed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether possession exits congestion cleanly.
Whether wide players remain outside until required.
Whether outside possession changes the defensive shape.
Whether central leads are timed effectively.
Whether attackers force corridor access.
Whether support arrives after the football re-enters the centre.
progressions: Allow defenders to transition after turnovers.
regressions: Widen the outside lanes and corridor gate.
Allow the coach to signal when inside access is available.
successIndicators: Use width to alter the defensive shape.
Identify safe opportunities to re-enter centrally.
Maintain attacking support after central access.
matchApplication: A team may win the football in a crowded central area but still need to move outside before attacking through the middle. This pattern creates space, moves defenders and reduces the risk of a turnover directly in front of goal.

title: Forward-Half Possession Lock
primarySkill: Maintaining attacking possession inside the forward half.
objective: Develop the attacking structure required to retain possession in the forward half while creating a higher-quality scoring opportunity.
groundSize: The forward half of the ground or an area approximately 65 metres long by full-ground width.
setup:
Use eight attackers against six defenders.
Position two attackers high, three across the middle forward area and three closer to goal.
Defenders organise inside the same area.
Begin possession near the forward-half boundary.
Mark a reset line approximately 55–60 metres from goal.
Attackers may recycle possession behind the reset line but may not leave the forward-half area.
Use the main goals.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins in possession near the forward-half boundary.
Attackers attempt to create a scoring opportunity through movement and controlled possession.
If the direct option is unavailable, the football may be recycled to a player near the reset line.
Forwards reposition as the football moves rather than remaining in fixed locations.
Defenders attempt to intercept and exit through either of two wide gates.
If the attackers lose possession, they apply immediate pressure to prevent the exit.
The attacking team scores normal match points.
It receives one bonus point for completing a controlled reset before creating a shot.
Defenders receive two points for exiting through a gate.
Play continues until a score, defensive exit or boundary turnover.
Rotate teams after three possessions.
coachingPoints: Maintain width and depth across the forward half.
Do not force a shot from a poor position.
Use the reset player to retain possession and move defenders.
Forwards must reposition when the football changes side.
Keep at least one dangerous option close to goal.
Attackers around the reset line should remain available without becoming flat.
Apply immediate pressure after a turnover.
Continue creating scoring options during recycled possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers maintain spacing during prolonged possession.
Whether the reset option remains available.
Whether forwards reposition after a switch.
Whether attackers force low-percentage shots.
Whether the team reacts immediately after losing possession.
Whether controlled possession creates improved scoring opportunities.
progressions: Reduce the size of the forward-half area.
Allow defenders to counterattack to the opposite goal.
Begin from a rushed or imperfect forward entry.
regressions: Fix one player as the reset option.
Pause after each reset to reorganise.
successIndicators: Use the reset option when required.
Prevent easy defensive exits after turnovers.
matchApplication: Teams frequently retain possession inside their forward half rather than forcing an immediate shot. Effective forward-half offence requires patience, structure and the ability to lock the football in when possession is lost.

title: Reset and Rebuild
primarySkill: Rebuilding attacking structure after forward movement is stopped.
objective: Teach players to recognise when forward progress has closed and reset possession so the team can rebuild width, depth and attacking options.
groundSize: A 60-metre-long by 45-metre-wide area divided into attacking, pressure and reset zones.
setup:
Mark a pressure zone across the middle of the area.
Mark a reset zone behind the starting possession.
Use eight attackers against five defenders.
Begin the football just before the pressure zone.
Position one or two attackers in the reset zone.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
Defenders begin compact inside the pressure zone.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move through the pressure zone.
Defenders close forward and central options.
If no safe forward option exists, the ball carrier disposes back to the reset zone.
As the football moves backwards, attackers spread and rebuild width and depth.
Defenders may advance but must remain goal side of their direct opponent.
The reset player transfers possession or identifies a new forward option.
Attackers then attempt to progress through the pressure zone again.
The team scores two points if a reset leads to successful progression through the final gate.
It scores one point for progressing without a reset.
Defenders score two points for intercepting a forced forward disposal.
Rotate defenders after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Recognise when forward options are unsafe.
Maintain a reliable player behind possession.
Reset early enough to avoid being trapped.
Spread immediately as the football moves backwards.
The reset player must scan before receiving.
Use the reset to change the angle or side of attack.
Rebuild depth rather than forming a flat line.
Attack again once the defensive shape has moved.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier recognises closed forward options.
Whether a reset player remains available.
Whether the team spreads during the backwards disposal.
Whether the reset changes the attacking picture.
Whether players attack again with improved shape.
Whether resets occur before possession becomes trapped.
progressions: Allow defenders to press fully into the reset zone.
Add a second layer of pressure.
regressions: Fix two players in the reset zone.
Pause after the reset to rebuild positions.
successIndicators: Recognise when forward movement is closed.
Preserve a support option behind possession.
Re-enter attack through a better angle.
matchApplication: Possession often reaches a point where the direct route is blocked. Strong attacking teams avoid forcing the football and instead reset through a teammate behind possession, rebuild their shape and attack from a new angle.

title: Boundary-to-Corridor Transfer
primarySkill: Transferring possession from the boundary side into a central attacking lane.
objective: Develop players’ ability to escape a restricted boundary position by creating a connected transfer into the corridor without exposing possession to unnecessary risk.
groundSize: A 60-metre-long by 50-metre-wide area with one boundary channel, one connecting lane and one corridor lane.
setup:
Mark a narrow boundary channel along one side.
Mark a central connecting lane.
Mark a corridor lane on the opposite side of the connecting lane.
Use eight attackers against five defenders.
Begin possession in the boundary channel.
Position one attacker behind the football, two in connecting positions and two further forward.
Defenders begin protecting the corridor.
Place a scoring gate at the far end of the corridor lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the boundary channel.
Attackers use short movement to maintain possession and draw defenders towards the boundary.
A connecting player leads into the central lane.
The football is transferred through the connecting player or a supporting player behind possession.
A second attacker moves into the corridor as the transfer begins.
The receiving player turns forward or releases immediately to the corridor runner.
Attackers score two points by transferring from the boundary and progressing through the corridor gate.
They score one point by continuing safely down the boundary.
Defenders score two points for intercepting a forced central transfer.
Reset from the opposite side after each repetition.
Rotate boundary, connection and corridor roles regularly.
coachingPoints: Do not leave the boundary until the connecting option is safe.
Move defenders towards the ball side before transferring.
Connecting players should lead on an angle.
Scan the corridor before receiving the first transfer.
Use support behind possession if the direct inside option is covered.
The corridor runner must arrive as the transfer is completed.
Deliver the football to the receiver’s forward side.
Continue boundary-side possession when central access is unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the attacking team draws defenders towards the boundary.
Whether connecting leads are timed effectively.
Whether the first inside receiver scans before possession.
Whether the corridor runner arrives at the correct moment.
Whether attackers force the transfer.
Whether support remains available behind the football.
progressions: Allow defenders to press the support player behind possession.
Begin from a kick-in or defensive-half turnover.
regressions: Fix the connecting player in a marked position.
Allow the coach to signal the transfer opportunity.
successIndicators: Move defenders before attempting the transfer.
matchApplication: Boundary possession can be safe but predictable. Teams need a controlled method of transferring back towards the corridor when the defensive shape allows it. The drill teaches players to create that opportunity rather than forcing a dangerous kick across the ground.

title: Team Offence Fundamentals Assessment
primarySkill: Applying fundamental team-offence principles in a live game environment.
objective: Assess whether players can independently apply the fundamental attacking principles developed in TO-001 to TO-019 during realistic, opposed play.
groundSize: Three-quarter ground or full ground depending on player numbers.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Use three-quarter ground for fewer than 24 players and full ground for larger squads.
Mark optional reference channels for width, corridor and boundary positions.
Begin play from varied starting situations including kick-ins, stoppages, defensive-half turnovers and centre possessions.
Use normal goals.
Assign coaches to observe attacking shape, support, tempo, corridor use and forward entry.
Allow normal legal contact appropriate to the playing group.
Do not provide tactical instructions during the first assessment block.
howTheDrillWorks:
Begin with one of the selected match-start scenarios.
The team in possession attempts to move the football into attack and score.
Players must independently establish width, depth and support around the football.
The attacking team may use fast movement, controlled possession, switches, resets or corridor access according to the defensive picture.
The defending team applies realistic pressure and attempts to transition after turnovers.
Normal match scoring applies.
Award one bonus point when the attacking team demonstrates a clearly successful offence principle, including:
A switch that creates open-side progression.
A reset that produces a better attacking entry.
A corridor entry created through movement rather than force.
A coordinated forward pattern that creates a clear scoring chance.
A clean contest release into numerical advantage.
Play in blocks of four to six minutes.
Record observations without stopping play during the first block.
Provide targeted feedback between blocks.
Repeat from a different starting scenario.
Complete a final block with no coach intervention.
coachingPoints: Establish shape immediately after winning possession.
Provide options ahead, beside and behind the football.
Maintain width without losing connection.
Use depth to avoid flat attacking structures.
Select tempo according to space and numbers.
Reset rather than force possession.
Access the corridor only when the option is safe.
Coordinate forward movement and scoring options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attacking shape forms without coach direction.
Whether players away from the football maintain width and depth.
Whether the ball carrier receives multiple disposal options.
Whether the team recognises when to attack quickly.
Whether players use resets and switches appropriately.
Whether corridor access is created rather than forced.
Whether forward movement remains coordinated.
Whether the team reacts effectively after turnovers.
progressions: Increase defensive numbers in selected areas.
Use full match rules and continuous play.
regressions: Pause between possessions for shape correction.
Assess one attacking principle at a time.
successIndicators: Use switches, releases and resets effectively.
Generate varied and high-quality scoring opportunities.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the fundamental team-offence behaviours required during match play. It allows coaches to determine whether players can recognise attacking problems, organise collectively and select effective solutions without constant instruction.

title: Give-and-Go Lane Exchange
primarySkill: Using give-and-go movement to exchange attacking lanes.
objective: Develop players’ ability to dispose, accelerate into a new lane and receive again without crowding the teammate who has taken possession.
groundSize: Three or four parallel lanes, each approximately 35 metres long and 8 metres wide.
setup:
Divide players into groups of three or four.
Position one group in each set of adjoining lanes.
The first player begins with the football in the central lane.
A second player starts five metres ahead in an outside lane.
A third player starts deeper in the opposite lane.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
Players may not remain in the same lane after disposing.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first player moves forward and disposes to the player in the outside lane.
Immediately after disposing, the first player accelerates across into the vacant lane ahead.
The receiver continues forward, draws towards the centre and returns the football to the original disposer.
The third player moves into the lane vacated by the receiver.
The group repeats the give-and-go pattern while exchanging lanes.
Players must maintain enough separation for each disposal to travel into space.
The group scores by moving the football through the end gate without two players occupying the same lane.
Players reset at the opposite end and repeat in reverse.
Rotate the starting ball carrier after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Dispose before changing lanes.
Accelerate immediately after releasing the football.
Move into space rather than following the receiver.
Keep support runners staggered.
Handball or kick to the receiver’s forward side.
Communicate the lane exchange early.
Maintain forward momentum throughout the sequence.
Avoid crossing directly in front of the ball carrier.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the disposer changes lanes immediately.
Whether players move into genuinely vacant space.
Whether two attackers cross into the same lane.
Whether disposals allow the receiver to maintain speed.
Whether support remains staggered.
Whether communication occurs before the lane exchange.
progressions: Add a passive defender in the central lane.
Allow the defender to choose which give-and-go option to close.
Require one kick during the sequence.
Continue into a live three-versus-two attack after the final gate.
regressions: Pause after each disposal to identify the vacant lane.
successIndicators: Exchange lanes without collision or crowding.
Deliver the football into the receiver’s path.
matchApplication: Give-and-go movement allows players to continue through defensive lines while changing the point of attack. Lane exchanges prevent defenders from tracking static opponents and create repeated support options around the football.

title: Third-Player Connection Run
primarySkill: Using a third player to connect two attacking teammates.
objective: Teach players to recognise when a third-player run can connect possession more safely and effectively than a direct disposal between two covered teammates.
groundSize: A 40-metre-long by 25-metre-wide area with two outside lanes and one central connection lane.
setup:
Divide players into groups of three attackers and one defender.
Position the ball carrier in one outside lane.
Position a target attacker further ahead in the opposite lane.
Place the third attacker behind the defender in the central lane.
The defender begins between the ball carrier and the forward target.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins moving forward in the outside lane.
The defender protects the direct disposal to the forward target.
The third attacker leads into the central connection lane.
The ball carrier disposes to the connecting player.
The forward target adjusts position and presents beyond the defender.
The connecting player turns or releases immediately to the forward target.
The original ball carrier follows to provide support behind.
Attackers score by moving through the end gate.
The defender scores by intercepting or forcing the football outside the area.
Repeat from the opposite side.
coachingPoints: The third player should arrive as the direct option becomes covered.
Lead into the receiver’s field of vision.
Present on an angle that allows the next disposal.
The ball carrier should recognise the direct lane is closed.
The connecting player must scan before receiving.
The forward target should move again after the connection begins.
The original disposer must remain involved.
Use the third player to improve the disposal angle, not slow the attack.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier identifies that the direct disposal is unsafe.
Whether the third player times the lead correctly.
Whether the connecting player receives side-on.
Whether the forward target adjusts after the first disposal.
Whether the original ball carrier supports behind.
Whether the sequence improves the attacking angle.
progressions: Allow the defender to change which lane is protected.
Require the connector to choose between turning, handballing or kicking.
regressions: Fix the connector in a marked position.
successIndicators: Recognise when the direct option is closed.
Receive in a position to continue forward.
matchApplication: A third-player connection is often required when direct attacking lanes are covered. It allows the team to change the angle of possession, move around a defender and continue forward without relying on a high-risk disposal.

title: Forward Handball Wave
primarySkill: Maintaining a forward-moving handball chain.
objective: Develop coordinated forward handball movement in which players release, continue running and create the next support option without becoming flat or congested.
groundSize: A 50-metre-long by 30-metre-wide channel.
setup:
Divide players into attacking groups of five or six.
Position attackers in two staggered waves.
Place two defenders between the starting line and scoring gate.
Begin the football with a player in the rear wave.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
Defenders begin with controlled pressure.
Use multiple channels where player numbers allow.
howTheDrillWorks:
The rear-wave player begins moving forward with the football.
Front-wave attackers provide angled handball options.
The ball carrier draws a defender and releases to a runner.
After disposing, the ball carrier continues forward to join the next wave.
The receiver carries briefly and selects another runner.
Attackers must remain staggered rather than moving level across the field.
The group scores by carrying or handballing through the scoring gate.
Defenders score by intercepting, forcing a fumble or stopping forward movement for five seconds.
Rotate defenders after three repetitions.
Repeat from different starting positions.
coachingPoints: Keep the wave staggered.
Draw pressure before releasing.
Handball into the runner’s path.
Continue running after disposal.
Provide one option ahead and another slightly behind or lateral.
Avoid every player sprinting ahead of the football.
Communicate the next option early.
Straighten the attack when space opens.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers remain at different depths.
Whether the ball carrier draws a defender.
Whether handballs are delivered to advantage.
Whether disposers continue running.
Whether the next support option appears before pressure arrives.
Whether the group maintains forward momentum.
progressions: Introduce one compulsory kick after the final handball.
Continue into a live forward-entry phase.
regressions: Permit players to pause before each disposal.
successIndicators: Reach the scoring gate with controlled forward speed.
matchApplication: Forward handball chains can break defensive lines when attackers run in connected waves. The pattern fails when players become flat, run ahead of possession or stop after disposal. This drill develops the movement required to sustain the chain.

title: Kick-Mark-Run Support Chain
primarySkill: Supporting a kick-mark possession chain with immediate movement.
objective: Teach players to move immediately after a marked disposal so the next receiver has connected options ahead, beside and behind.
groundSize: A 60-metre-long by 35-metre-wide area with four staggered receiving zones.
setup:
Mark four staggered receiving zones through the area.
Position one or two players in each zone.
Begin the football at one end.
Players may lead out of their zone but must be replaced by another attacker.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
No defenders are used initially.
Use a second football if player numbers are high.
howTheDrillWorks:
The starting player kicks to a leading player in the next zone.
After kicking, the disposer runs forward to provide support behind or beside the receiver.
The player who marks scans ahead before playing on.
Another attacker leads from the next zone.
A third attacker rotates into the space vacated by the leader.
The chain continues through all zones.
The group scores by completing the final kick or carry through the scoring gate.
Players reset from the opposite end.
Rotate starting positions after each repetition.
Introduce a five-second possession limit once movement is consistent.
coachingPoints: Kick to the receiver’s advantage.
Move immediately after kicking.
The marker should scan before the football arrives.
Lead from one space and clear it for a replacement.
Maintain an option behind possession.
Avoid waiting until the mark is taken before beginning the next lead.
Use angled leads to preserve the following disposal lane.
Keep the chain connected at all times.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the kicker moves after disposal.
Whether the next lead begins early.
Whether vacated space is replaced.
Whether the marker has more than one option.
Whether kicks allow the receiver to continue.
Whether the chain remains connected between zones.
progressions: Add passive defenders in alternate zones.
Allow defenders to close the first option.
Require one switch of play during the chain.
Continue live after a dropped mark.
regressions: Pause to rebuild the shape after each mark.
successIndicators: Begin the next lead before the mark is completed.
Complete the chain without losing attacking shape.
matchApplication: Controlled kick-mark possession still requires constant movement. When players stop after disposal or wait for the mark before leading, the team loses momentum and becomes predictable. This drill develops continuous support around controlled possession.

title: High Half-Forward Rotation
primarySkill: Rotating players through high half-forward connection roles.
objective: Develop coordinated movement between midfielders and high half-forwards so the team maintains a reliable connection between the centre of the ground and the forward line.
groundSize: An area extending from the centre square to approximately 25 metres from goal.
setup:
Position three midfield attackers between the centre and attacking 50.
Position two high half-forwards near the 50-metre arc.
Position two deeper forwards closer to goal.
Add four defenders across the midfield and high-forward areas.
Begin the football near the centre.
Mark two wide high-half-forward channels.
Use the main goals or a scoring gate.
howTheDrillWorks:
Midfielders begin moving possession towards attack.
One high half-forward leads towards the football in a wide channel.
The second high half-forward holds deeper or rotates towards the opposite side.
When the first high half-forward receives, a midfielder runs past or replaces the vacated high position.
The receiving half-forward may turn, release to the runner or switch to the opposite side.
Deeper forwards coordinate their movement according to the side of entry.
The attack continues until a shot, turnover or defensive exit.
After each repetition, rotate midfielders and high half-forwards.
Restart from the opposite side.
Increase defensive pressure as the rotations improve.
coachingPoints: Only one high half-forward should lead into the immediate ball-side space.
The opposite half-forward must preserve width and depth.
A midfielder should replace the vacated connection position.
High half-forwards should receive facing the attacking goal where possible.
Do not allow every forward to lead at the same time.
Coordinate deeper forward movement with the high connection.
Communicate the rotation before possession arrives.
Continue moving after the first connection.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first high half-forward creates a clear connection.
Whether the opposite player maintains useful space.
Whether midfielders replace vacated positions.
Whether the receiver can continue forward.
Whether deeper forwards react to the side of possession.
Whether rotations occur without crowding.
progressions: Allow the defending team to counterattack fully.
regressions: Fix one high half-forward in each channel.
Reduce the length of the area.
Coach the rotation verbally during early repetitions.
successIndicators: Continue the attack without a structural gap.
matchApplication: High half-forwards often provide the critical link between midfield possession and forward entry. Effective rotation prevents that area from becoming empty after a lead and allows midfielders to continue running into dangerous positions.

title: Midfield Spread from Possession
primarySkill: Spreading from a central possession to create multiple attacking lanes.
objective: Teach midfielders to separate quickly after possession is won so the ball carrier receives forward, lateral and release options instead of immediate congestion.
groundSize: A 45-metre-long by 40-metre-wide area with a central contest square and three forward lanes.
setup:
Mark a central contest square approximately 12 metres by 12 metres.
Mark left, central and right attacking lanes beyond the square.
Place three attackers and three defenders inside the contest square.
Position two attacking receivers outside the square.
Place a scoring gate at the far end of each lane.
Begin each repetition with a ball-up or ground-ball feed.
Rotate inside and outside roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players contest the football inside the central square.
As possession is won, midfield attackers spread into different lanes.
One player provides immediate short support.
One player accelerates forward.
One player remains behind or lateral as a release option.
The ball winner selects the safest attacking lane.
Outside receivers join the movement and provide the next connection.
