matchApplication: Ground-ball wins create brief attacking opportunities while defenders remain concentrated around the contest. Fast, coordinated spread allows the team to turn a difficult possession into a forward surge.
relatedDrills: GB-120 – Ground Balls Chapter Final Assessment

title: Broken-Tackle Support
primarySkill: Supporting a teammate who breaks or absorbs a tackle.
objective: Develop players’ ability to anticipate contact and provide immediate attacking support when a ball carrier breaks, rides or partially escapes a tackle.
groundSize: A 35-metre-long by 20-metre-wide channel with one contact zone and two support lanes.
setup:
Mark a contact zone approximately eight metres long.
Position one ball carrier at the beginning of the zone.
Place one controlled defender or tackle-bag holder inside.
Position two attacking support runners behind and on separate angles.
Place a second defender beyond the contact zone.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
Rotate all roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier enters the contact zone.
The defender applies controlled tackling or body pressure.
The ball carrier attempts to maintain balance and protect possession.
Support runners remain connected on separate angles.
If the ball carrier breaks free, one runner accelerates ahead while the second remains available behind.
If the ball carrier is slowed, possession is released to the safest support runner.
The second defender attempts to close the next possession.
Attackers score by progressing through the scoring gate.
Defenders score by completing the tackle, forcing a turnover or stopping movement for five seconds.
Repeat from both sides.
coachingPoints: Support runners should anticipate contact rather than wait for the outcome.
Maintain different depths around the ball carrier.
The ball carrier must protect the football through contact.
Release before balance or control is lost.
If the tackle is broken, support should accelerate into the newly created space.
Avoid running directly behind the ball carrier.
Communicate the available release side.
Continue supporting through the second defender.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether support remains connected before contact.
Whether runners maintain separate angles.
Whether the ball carrier protects possession.
Whether the decision to break or release is made early enough.
Whether support accelerates after a broken tackle.
Whether the attack remains connected against the second defender.
progressions: Replace the pad with a live controlled tackler.
Allow the second defender to begin closer.
Continue into a live scoring phase.
successIndicators: Use the space created by the tackle.
matchApplication: A tackle can temporarily remove both the ball carrier and defender from the play. Connected support allows the attacking team to exploit the space created, whether the tackle is broken or possession must be released.
relatedDrills: TK-120 – Tackling and Pressure Chapter Final Assessment

title: Second-Effort Attack
primarySkill: Re-entering the attacking phase after an initial skill error or contest loss.
objective: Teach players to respond immediately to a dropped mark, fumble, smother or lost contest and rebuild the attacking possession through a second effort.
groundSize: A 40-metre-long by 30-metre-wide area with a contested reception zone and scoring gate.
setup:
Position one attacking receiver and one defender inside a marked reception zone.
Position three attacking support players around the zone.
Position two additional defenders nearby.
Place a feeder 20–25 metres away.
Mark a scoring gate beyond the contest.
The feeder varies the quality and type of disposal.
Rotate all roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers the football to the contested reception zone.
The receiver attempts to mark or gather under pressure.
The feed may intentionally create a fumble, spoil, bounce or difficult pickup.
All players react immediately to the actual outcome.
If the attacker controls possession, the group connects towards the scoring gate.
If possession is lost or spilled, attackers apply pressure and attempt to regain it.
The original receiver must make a second effort rather than stopping.
Attackers score two points for recovering the football and reaching the gate.
They score one point for a clean first-possession attack.
Defenders score by winning possession and exiting through a side gate.
Reset after each outcome.
coachingPoints: Expect an imperfect outcome.
React to the football rather than the previous mistake.
The original player must recover immediately.
Support players should maintain inside and outside coverage.
One player attacks the loose football while others support.
Apply pressure if defenders gain first possession.
Rebuild attacking shape as soon as possession is regained.
Avoid emotional or physical pause after an error.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players stop after an error.
Whether the original receiver makes a second effort.
Whether support remains balanced.
Whether one attacker takes responsibility for the loose football.
Whether possession is reorganised after recovery.
Whether defensive exits are pressured.
progressions: Increase the difficulty of the initial feed.
Add a scoreboard and time-pressure scenario.
matchApplication: Australian football possessions are rarely perfect. Teams that respond quickest to mistakes, spills and smothers can recover the football and continue attacking before the opposition gains control.
relatedDrills: GB-120 – Ground Balls Chapter Final Assessment

title: Outnumbered Possession Survival
primarySkill: Retaining possession while temporarily outnumbered.
objective: Develop players’ ability to protect and retain the football until additional support arrives during a temporary attacking outnumber.
groundSize: A 40-metre-long by 35-metre-wide area with a possession zone and two support-entry gates.
setup:
Begin with four attackers against five defenders inside the possession area.
Position two additional attackers outside separate support-entry gates.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
The outside attackers may enter after a coach signal or completed possession target.
Defenders apply realistic pressure but must use legal contact.
Rotate teams after each three-possession block.
howTheDrillWorks:
The four attackers begin in possession while outnumbered.
They attempt to retain the football using width, support behind possession and controlled tempo.
Defenders press and attempt to force a turnover.
After four completed disposals, one outside attacker may enter.
After a further two disposals, the second support player may enter.
Once the numbers become even or favourable, attackers may progress towards the scoring gate.
Attackers score two points for surviving the outnumber and reaching the gate.
They score one point for retaining possession for eight disposals.
Defenders score two points for forcing a turnover before support arrives.
On turnover, defenders attack towards the opposite end.
Restart with new outside support players.
coachingPoints: Recognise that immediate forward attack may be unsafe.
Protect possession and avoid low-percentage disposals.
Maintain width despite being outnumbered.
Keep at least one support option behind the football.
Use movement to prevent defenders from covering multiple attackers.
Communicate when support is entering.
Change tempo once the numerical position improves.
Do not remain passive after support arrives.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers recognise the outnumber.
Whether possession is protected rather than forced forward.
Whether attackers maintain useful spacing.
Whether support behind possession remains available.
Whether new players enter into useful positions.
Whether the team accelerates once numbers improve.
progressions: Remove the disposal-count signal and use a coach’s visual cue.
Extend the area to three-quarter ground.
successIndicators: Change from survival to attack at the correct moment.
matchApplication: Teams regularly face temporary outnumbers after turnovers, contests or positional movement. Retaining possession until support arrives prevents unnecessary turnovers and allows the attacking phase to restart from a stronger position.

title: Smother Recovery Connection
primarySkill: Recovering and reconnecting after an attacking disposal is smothered.
objective: Teach players to react immediately to a smothered kick or handball and create a connected second attacking possession.
groundSize: A 35-metre-long by 25-metre-wide area with a disposal zone and two recovery lanes.
setup:
Position one ball carrier inside the disposal zone.
Position one defender close enough to pressure or smother.
Place two attacking support players in separate recovery lanes.
Position one additional defender beyond the zone.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
The initial defender alternates between allowing the disposal and attempting a controlled smother.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives and prepares to dispose.
The defender applies immediate pressure and may attempt a controlled smother.
Support players remain active on separate angles.
If the disposal clears the defender, play continues towards the scoring gate.
If the football is smothered, the ball carrier and support players react immediately.
The nearest attacker attempts to recover the loose football.
Other attackers provide outside and rear support.
The second defender applies pressure to the recovery possession.
Attackers score two points for recovering the smother and reaching the gate.
Defenders score by winning the loose football and exiting through a side gate.
Reset after each outcome.
coachingPoints: Expect pressure on the disposal.
Support should remain active until the football clears the contest.
The original disposer must react immediately to the smother.
One player attacks the loose football while others spread.
Protect the recovery possession before releasing.
Avoid repeating the same blocked disposal line.
Use the recovery to change the attacking angle.
Apply pressure immediately if defenders win the loose football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether support players stop when the disposal begins.
Whether the original disposer reacts after the smother.
Whether one attacker takes responsibility for recovery.
Whether support forms on different angles.
Whether the next disposal avoids the original pressure line.
Whether defensive possession is pressured.
progressions: Make the smother defender fully active.
Continue into a live scoring phase.
Add repeated smother and spoil scenarios.
regressions: Predetermine whether the disposal will be smothered.
matchApplication: Smothers create unpredictable loose footballs and rapid changes in advantage. Teams that react first and remain connected can recover the possession and continue attacking before defenders reorganise.

title: Intercept Denial Movement
primarySkill: Moving and disposing to reduce intercept opportunities.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise intercept danger and adjust leading patterns, disposal direction and support positions to retain attacking possession.
groundSize: A 55-metre-long by 40-metre-wide area with three attacking lanes and an intercept zone.
setup:
Mark three vertical attacking lanes.
Use seven attackers against five defenders.
Position one defender as a designated interceptor between the starting possession and the scoring end.
Position other defenders on direct opponents.
Begin the football at one end.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
The interceptor may leave their player to attack predictable disposals.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession at one end.
Attackers create staggered leads across different lanes.
The interceptor scans the ball carrier and attempts to leave their opponent.
The ball carrier must recognise intercept danger before disposing.
Attackers may use a short connection, lateral pass, reset or kick to the receiver’s safe side.
Players away from the football move to occupy the interceptor or create another option.
The attacking team scores by progressing through the far gate.
A completed intercept earns the defending team two points.
A spoil or forced turnover earns one point.
Rotate the designated interceptor after three repetitions.
Restart from varying positions.
coachingPoints: Scan defenders who can leave their direct opponent.
Do not kick over a defender positioned in the disposal lane.
Leads should move away from the interceptor’s preferred space.
Deliver the football to the receiver’s protected side.
Use short possession to draw the interceptor out.
Players away from the football can occupy dangerous defenders.
Reset when the intended lane becomes unsafe.
Avoid slow, high disposals that invite interception.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier scans beyond the direct opponent.
Whether leading patterns separate from the interceptor.
Whether attackers occupy dangerous defenders.
Whether disposals are directed to the receiver’s advantage.
Whether players reset rather than force the football.
Whether the same predictable lane is repeatedly used.
progressions: Allow defenders to rotate interceptor responsibility.
regressions: Identify the intercept defender before each repetition.
matchApplication: Intercept defenders can control attacking movement when the ball carrier focuses only on the intended target. Effective offence manipulates these defenders, changes angles and delivers the football away from their influence.

title: Repeat Forward Entry
primarySkill: Rebuilding and delivering a second forward entry after the first entry is repelled.
objective: Teach players to regain possession after a defensive clearance and reorganise quickly for a more effective repeat forward entry.
groundSize: The attacking half of the ground using full width.
setup:
Use eight attackers against seven defenders.
Position attackers across high-forward, wing and deeper-forward roles.
Position defenders inside the forward half.
Begin possession 55–70 metres from goal.
Mark two defensive exit gates near the wings.
Use normal goals.
Assign two attackers as high defenders responsible for retaining the football after a clearance.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team delivers an initial forward entry.
Defenders attempt to mark, spoil or win possession.
If defenders gain possession, they attempt to exit through either wide gate.
High attackers apply pressure and attempt to intercept or recover the clearance.
If the attacking team regains possession, players must rebuild forward structure.
Deep forwards reset their leading lanes rather than repeating the first movement.
The team delivers a second forward entry from the new possession point.
Normal match scoring applies.
Award one bonus point for a repeat entry that creates a controlled shot.
Defenders score two points for a clean exit.
Continue until a score, defensive exit or second turnover.
Rotate teams after four possessions.
coachingPoints: Anticipate the likely defensive exit.
High attackers should maintain width and depth behind the first entry.
Apply immediate but organised pressure after a defensive win.
Do not send every attacker towards the clearance.
Reset forward leading patterns after possession is regained.
Use the new entry angle rather than repeating the first kick.
Maintain a player behind the recovered possession.
Select a composed second entry.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers anticipate defensive exits.
Whether forward-half spacing remains balanced.
Whether pressure is applied without crowding.
Whether regained possession is secured before re-entry.
Whether forwards reset their movement.
Whether the second entry improves on the first.
progressions: Allow defenders to counterattack towards the opposite goal.
regressions: Limit defensive exits to one gate.
Use passive pressure after the clearance.
matchApplication: Many scores result from repeat forward entries rather than the initial attack. Teams must retain structure behind the football, recover defensive exits and deliver again before the opposition can reorganise.

title: Chaos Possession Reorganisation
primarySkill: Reorganising attacking structure after unpredictable possession changes.
objective: Develop players’ ability to rapidly establish attacking width, depth and connection after an unpredictable contest, deflection or turnover.
groundSize: A 55-metre-long by 45-metre-wide area with scoring gates at both ends.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Use six to nine players per team depending on numbers.
Place scoring gates at both ends.
Position the coach outside the area with multiple footballs.
Begin players in a loose neutral structure.
The coach may introduce possession through a ground ball, high ball, deflection, handball or kick.
No fixed positions are assigned.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach introduces a football unpredictably into the playing area.
Both teams compete to win possession.
The team that gains control must immediately establish attacking shape.
Players spread to create width, depth and support behind the football.
The attacking team attempts to score through either gate nominated by the coach or determined by possession direction.
If possession changes, the new attacking team reorganises immediately.
The coach may whistle and introduce a second football after the first leaves play.
Bonus points are awarded for:
Establishing three clear disposal options within three seconds.
Switching from congestion into width.
Resetting successfully after immediate pressure.
Scoring after a second-effort recovery.
Play in intense blocks of 60–90 seconds.
Allow sufficient recovery between blocks.
Rotate starting positions before each block.
coachingPoints: Identify possession direction immediately.
Spread as soon as control is established.
Create options ahead, beside and behind.
Communicate roles without waiting for coach instruction.
Select fast attack when defenders are unbalanced.
Reset when possession is unstable.
Avoid every player chasing the football.
Maintain decision quality despite fatigue and unpredictability.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly teams recognise possession.
Whether attacking structure forms within seconds.
Whether players away from the football spread.
Whether support appears at different depths.
Whether teams select the appropriate tempo.
Whether players reorganise after repeated possession changes.
Whether fatigue causes crowding or rushed disposal.
progressions: Introduce a second live football briefly.
regressions: Pause after the contest to establish shape.
matchApplication: Match play regularly becomes chaotic through spills, smothers, deflections and rapid turnovers. Teams that organise first can turn unstable possession into a clear attacking advantage.

title: Pressure and Contest Mastery Assessment
primarySkill: Applying complete attacking structure through pressure, contact and unpredictable contests.
objective: Assess whether players can consistently convert pressured and unstable possession into connected team offence across repeated match-like phases.
groundSize: Three-quarter ground or full ground.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Use three-quarter ground for smaller squads and full ground for larger groups.
Use normal goals.
Prepare varied starting situations:
Boundary pressure.
Ground-ball contest.
Aerial contest.
Smothered disposal.
Temporary attacking outnumber.
Defensive clearance and repeat entry.
Unpredictable loose football.
Assign coaches to observe contest exit, support shape, decision quality, second effort and forward connection.
Apply legal match-like pressure appropriate to the playing group.
Provide no tactical coaching during the opening assessment block.
howTheDrillWorks:
Begin each possession from one of the prepared pressure or contest scenarios.
The team that wins possession attempts to establish connected offence and score.
Players must provide support ahead, beside and behind the football.
The attacking team may release wide, reset, switch, surge forward or retain possession according to the defensive picture.
Normal match scoring applies.
Award one bonus point for each clearly successful action:
Escaping boundary pressure through a controlled inside release.
Converting a ground-ball win into a forward surge.
Supporting a broken tackle or contact release.
Recovering a smother, spoil or skill error.
Surviving a temporary outnumber until support arrives.
Avoiding an intercept defender through movement or disposal adjustment.
Producing a controlled repeat forward entry.
The defending team attacks immediately after turnovers.
Play in blocks of five to seven minutes.
Coaches record observations without stopping the opening block.
Provide concise feedback between blocks.
Change the starting scenario for each block.
Complete the final block from unpredictable coach feeds and match restarts.
Finish with no coach intervention.
coachingPoints: Secure the football before accelerating.
Protect possession through contact.
Maintain support outside congestion.
Recognise when to attack and when to retain possession.
Produce second efforts after errors or defensive actions.
Adjust movement to intercept danger.
Rebuild forward structure after repeat entries.
Organise immediately after unpredictable possession changes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players remain composed through contact.
Whether support appears at multiple angles.
Whether attackers recognise temporary outnumbers.
Whether possession is retained when immediate attack is unsafe.
Whether second efforts occur automatically.
Whether intercept danger changes attacking movement.
Whether repeat forward entries are organised.
Whether players establish shape after chaotic possession changes.
Whether skill execution and communication survive fatigue.
Whether transition response is immediate after turnovers.
progressions: Increase match-like contact and defensive pressure.
regressions: Limit each block to one pressure scenario.
Pause between possessions for structural review.
successIndicators: Win or retain possession under pressure.
Select safe and effective contest exits.
Convert ground-ball and contact wins into forward movement.
Organise quickly after chaotic possession changes.
Maintain decision quality under match-like fatigue.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the pressure and contest behaviours developed through TO-041 to TO-059. It determines whether players can sustain effective team offence when possession is unstable, contact is realistic and attacking decisions must be made under genuine match pressure.

title: Defensive-Half Exit Width
primarySkill: Creating width to exit the defensive half.
objective: Develop players’ ability to establish wide, connected options that allow the team to move possession safely from the defensive half into open field.
groundSize: The defensive half of the ground using full width, with two exit gates positioned near the wings.
setup:
Use eight attackers against six defenders.
Begin possession inside defensive 50.
Position two attackers in wide pockets, two across half-back and two higher near the wings.
Position one or two attackers as central or rear support.
Defenders begin in a compact central shape.
Mark one exit gate on each wing approximately 55–65 metres from goal.
Use normal kick-in rules or begin from a controlled mark.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins in possession inside defensive 50.
Wide players move early to stretch the defensive shape.
Half-backs provide staggered short and intermediate options.
Central players remain available without crowding the corridor.
The ball carrier selects a safe exit through width, a controlled central connection or a reset.
Defenders attempt to compress the preferred side and force a rushed disposal.
Attackers score one point for reaching a wing gate under control.
They score two points if the exit uses one side before transferring to the opposite wing gate.
Defenders score two points for winning possession inside defensive 50.
On turnover, defenders attempt to score at the main goals.
Restart from the opposite side after each completed exit.
Rotate wide, central and defensive roles regularly.
coachingPoints: Establish width before the ball carrier is pressured.
Use staggered options rather than a flat line across half-back.
Maintain one safe support option behind possession.
Wide players should lead into space rather than wait stationary.
Avoid forcing central possession when defenders remain compact.
Move the defence with short possession before switching.
Accelerate once the football reaches the open side.
Continue supporting after the first exit disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether wide players establish position early.
Whether half-backs provide options at different depths.
Whether the ball carrier scans both sides.
Whether support remains behind possession.
Whether attackers force the corridor.
Whether the team increases speed after creating the open side.
progressions: Allow defenders to begin in a balanced full-width structure.
Begin from a turnover rather than a controlled mark.
Continue play through to a forward entry.
regressions: Fix wide receivers in starting zones.
Pause after each disposal to rebuild shape.
successIndicators: Connect the exit to the next attacking phase.
matchApplication: Defensive-half offence requires width, patience and connected support. Teams that stretch the opposition can escape pressure, avoid dangerous central turnovers and launch attacks through the wings or open side.

title: Layered Kick-In Exit
primarySkill: Creating layered options from a kick-in.
objective: Teach players to provide short, intermediate and long kick-in options that allow the team to exit defensive 50 without relying on one predictable target.
groundSize: Defensive 50 extending to approximately 70 metres from goal, using full width.
setup:
Use seven attackers against five defenders.
Position a designated kick-in player in the goal square.
Place one short option in each pocket.
Position two intermediate players across half-back.
Position two longer targets near the wings.
Defenders begin in a zone selected by the coach.
Mark an exit line approximately 65–70 metres from goal.
Rotate the kick-in player after every two repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kick-in player begins after a behind or coach signal.
Short options lead to opposite pockets.
Intermediate options adjust according to defender movement.
Long targets remain separated and provide width.
The kick-in player scans all three layers before disposing.
If the short option is used, the remaining attackers rotate to create the next exit.
If the intermediate or long option is selected, support forms ahead and behind the receiver.
Attackers score one point for crossing the exit line under control.
They score two points for completing the exit without using the same first option in consecutive repetitions.
Defenders score two points for a turnover inside defensive 50.
On turnover, defenders attack the main goals.
Reset with a different defensive shape.
coachingPoints: Provide options at three different depths.
Short players should lead rather than wait beside the goal square.
Intermediate players must remain visible to the kicker.
Long targets should stay separated.
Scan before leaving the goal square.
The unused layers must reposition after the first disposal.
Support the receiver from behind and ahead.
Avoid repeating the same exit pattern regardless of defence.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether all three layers are available.
Whether players move in response to defenders.
Whether the kicker scans before committing.
Whether unused options rotate after the first kick.
Whether the receiver has support.
Whether the exit pattern becomes predictable.
progressions: Allow defenders to press the goal square more aggressively.
Begin immediately after a live behind.
Continue play through the centre and into attack.
regressions: Allow the kick-in player extra time.
successIndicators: Adjust movement to the defensive shape.
Cross the exit line without a dangerous turnover.
matchApplication: A predictable kick-in allows the opposition to compress one target or side. Layered movement gives the kicker several options and allows the team to adapt to different defensive zones and pressure.

title: Half-Back Connection Diamond
primarySkill: Maintaining a connection diamond across half-back.
objective: Develop a four-player half-back structure that provides forward, lateral and rear options while the team moves possession out of defence.
groundSize: A 50-metre-long by 45-metre-wide defensive-half area.
setup:
Position four attackers in a diamond:
One rear player.
Two wide half-backs.
One higher central connection.
Add two additional attacking targets further ahead.
Use four defenders.
Begin possession with the rear player or either wide half-back.
Mark an exit gate at the far end.
Players may rotate through the diamond after disposal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession at the rear of the diamond.
Defenders close one or more connections.
The ball carrier selects a wide, forward or opposite-side option.
After disposing, the player moves to replace another point of the diamond.
The other attackers adjust to maintain four connected points.
The higher connection may lead forward or return towards possession.
Once the football reaches a forward target, the diamond advances behind the play.
Attackers score by moving through the exit gate with the diamond still connected.
Defenders score by intercepting or isolating the ball carrier for five seconds.
Rotate defenders and starting positions after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Maintain one player behind possession.
Keep two lateral options available where possible.
The high point should remain connected without becoming too close.
Rotate after disposal rather than leaving the structure empty.
Receive with body position open to the field.
Use the rear player to change direction.
Advance the entire diamond as possession moves forward.
Communicate positional replacements.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether all four points remain connected.
Whether the rear player remains available.
Whether wide players preserve separation.
Whether the high player adjusts depth.
Whether disposers rotate.
Whether the diamond advances rather than remaining deep.
progressions: Allow defenders to transition after turnovers.
Connect the drill to a wing or corridor attack.
regressions: Pause after each disposal to restore shape.
successIndicators: Provide forward, lateral and rear support.
Exit the defensive area without isolating possession.
matchApplication: A half-back diamond provides multiple safe disposal angles and allows a team to transfer possession without losing forward connection. The structure is especially useful against compact defensive pressure.

title: Wing Connection Ladder
primarySkill: Building staggered connections along the wing.
objective: Teach players to create a sequence of staggered wing options that allows controlled advancement without becoming trapped against the boundary.
groundSize: A 70-metre-long by 25-metre-wide wing channel with four staggered receiving zones.
setup:
Mark four staggered receiving zones along the wing.
Position one or two attackers in each zone.
Add four defenders throughout the channel.
Begin possession at the defensive end.
Mark an inside support strip along the edge of the wing channel.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
Players may leave a zone after disposal but must be replaced.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins at the defensive end.
The first receiver leads within or out of the opening zone.
The next player provides a higher option at a different depth.
An inside support player remains available to prevent boundary trapping.
After each mark or possession, the disposer moves forward or inside.
Another attacker replaces the vacated zone.
Defenders attempt to force possession towards the boundary.
Attackers may continue along the wing or use the inside strip to change the angle.
The team scores by moving through the far gate.
Defenders score by forcing the football outside or winning possession.
Reset in the opposite direction.
Rotate defenders after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Stagger options along the wing.
Maintain one inside support player.
Lead into space rather than standing beside the boundary.
Replace vacated receiving zones.
Avoid kicking over multiple connected options unless the long target is clearly free.
Receive side-on where possible.
Continue moving after marking.
Use the inside support before the boundary becomes a trap.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether wing options remain staggered.
Whether inside support is available.
Whether zones are replaced.
Whether the ball carrier becomes trapped near the boundary.
Whether players scan inside before disposing.
Whether the team maintains forward connection.
regressions: Increase the width of the channel.
Pause to restore the ladder after each disposal.
matchApplication: Wing ball movement requires connection at several depths and an inside escape option. Without this structure, possession becomes predictable and can be trapped against the boundary.

title: Centre-Square Bypass Transfer
primarySkill: Moving possession around a blocked central area.
objective: Develop players’ ability to bypass a congested centre square through connected outside possession before re-entering the attacking corridor.
groundSize: An area from defensive half-back to attacking half-forward using full ground width, with the centre square marked as a pressure zone.
setup:
Use ten attackers against seven defenders.
Mark the centre square as a restricted pressure zone.
Position defenders compactly around and inside the square.
Begin possession at half-back.
Place attackers across both wings and high half-forward.
Mark a corridor re-entry gate beyond the centre square.
Attackers may not enter the centre square during the first phase.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins at half-back.
Defenders protect the centre square and immediate corridor.
Attackers move possession towards either wing.
Supporting players behind the football maintain switch options.
The team attempts to bypass the square through outside connections.
Once possession moves beyond the square, attackers may re-enter the corridor through the marked gate.
High half-forwards adjust to provide inside and outside options.
Attackers score two points for bypassing the square and re-entering through the corridor gate.
They score one point for progressing entirely along the wing.
Defenders score two points for winning possession in the central pressure area.
On turnover, defenders attack the opposite direction.
Reset from alternating half-back positions.
coachingPoints: Accept that the direct central route may be unavailable.
Establish outside connection early.
Maintain support behind possession for a switch.
Move defenders laterally before attempting re-entry.
Do not allow outside movement to become slow or static.
High players should prepare the corridor re-entry.
Scan inside before receiving on the wing.
Re-enter centrally only after moving beyond the defensive block.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers accept the blocked central route.
Whether outside connections remain close enough.
Whether support behind possession is maintained.
Whether the defence is moved laterally.
Whether corridor re-entry is timed after the bypass.
Whether wing players scan inside before receiving.
progressions: Allow attackers to enter the centre square when they believe it is safe.
Add another defender outside the square.
Continue through to a scoring attempt.
regressions: Pause once possession moves beyond the square.
successIndicators: Re-enter the corridor beyond the defensive block.
matchApplication: When the centre square and corridor are heavily defended, teams need to move around the block rather than force possession through it. Outside transfer can create safer central access further up the ground.

title: Three-Line Switch and Advance
primarySkill: Switching possession while advancing all three playing lines.
objective: Teach defenders, midfielders and forwards to shift collectively during a switch so the team remains connected and ready to attack from the open side.
groundSize: Three-quarter ground using full width, divided into defensive, midfield and forward zones.
setup:
Divide the ground into defensive, midfield and forward zones.
Use twelve attackers against eight defenders.
Begin possession in one side of the defensive zone.
Position attackers across all three zones.
Defenders begin compressed towards the ball side.
Use normal goals or a forward scoring gate.
Players may move between zones after the switch begins.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession on one side of the defensive zone.

Defenders transition immediately after turnovers.

Defensive players should advance behind possession.
Midfielders must provide one inside and one outside connection.
Forwards should adjust before the football reaches the open side.
Maintain different depths across all three lines.

Accelerate forward once the switch is complete.
Keep rear support during the advancement.

Whether forwards adjust early.

Use eight attackers against six defenders.
Mark a pressure zone across the middle.
Mark a reset zone behind the starting possession.
Position two attackers inside the reset zone.
Position forward targets beyond the pressure zone.
Begin possession immediately before the pressure zone.

howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with forward possession.
Defenders close the direct lanes.
The ball carrier disposes backwards into the reset zone.
As the football travels backwards, attackers spread across the width.
Forward targets clear old leading lanes and prepare new ones.
The reset player transfers the football or identifies the newly opened forward option.

Spread immediately as possession moves backwards.

Whether attackers spread as possession moves backwards.
Whether forward targets create new lanes.
Whether the reset changes the attack angle.
Whether the team accelerates after the reset.
Whether repeated backwards possessions become passive.

Begin possession in the central channel.
Position two attackers in each outside channel.
Position remaining attackers centrally and behind possession.
Defenders begin in a balanced shape.
Place a scoring gate at the far end of each outside channel.
Attackers may move between channels after the first disposal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins centrally.
The ball carrier identifies which outside channel has the weaker defensive coverage.
Two central attackers run towards that channel at different depths.
Existing outside players hold width and prepare to connect.
Possession is transferred into the overloaded channel.
Attackers use their numerical advantage through kick, handball or overlap.
One central or weak-side player remains behind possession.
The team scores two points for creating and using a clear numbers-up situation through an outside gate.
It scores one point for progressing through any gate.
Defenders score two points for trapping the football in the overloaded channel.

Move extra players at different depths.

title: Corridor-to-Outside Release

Position two attackers in each outside release channel.
Position defenders to compress the corridor after the first disposal.
Mark one scoring gate at the end of each outside channel.
Keep one attacking support player behind the central possession.
Restart from varied central positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession inside the corridor.
Defenders close around the central ball carrier.
Outside attackers hold width and move into the ball carrier’s vision.
The central player may continue forward if the corridor remains open.

coachingPoints: Central possession is valuable but must not be forced.

Wide players should hold their space until required.

title: Team Ball Movement Mid-Block Assessment

Divide players into two balanced teams.

Begin possessions from varied locations:

Defensive-half mark.
Boundary possession.
Half-back turnover.
Central congestion.
Wing possession.

Assign coaches to observe defensive-half structure, line connection, switches, resets and attacking progression.
Allow realistic legal pressure.

howTheDrillWorks:

Players must provide width, depth and support behind possession.
The team may use:

A half-back diamond.
A wing connection ladder.
A switch across all three lines.
A backwards-then-forward reset.
An outside overload.
A corridor-to-outside release.
Normal match scoring applies.

Controlled defensive-half exit.

successIndicators: Exit the defensive half with control.
Maintain width, depth and rear support.
Connect defensive, midfield and forward lines.

Create and use outside numerical advantages.
Release central possession before becoming trapped.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the team-ball-movement principles developed through TO-061 to TO-069. It measures whether players can move possession from defence into attack while maintaining connection, adapting to defensive pressure and selecting the appropriate route through the ground.

title: High-Wing Inboard Chain
primarySkill: Connecting wing possession back towards the inside of the ground.
objective: Develop players’ ability to use a high-wing possession to create a safe inboard connection and continue attacking through a more dangerous central lane.

title: Deep Switch with Central Hold

howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession in the defensive half.

Defenders transition immediately after turnovers.

Restart from a different defensive-half situation.
Reduce the attacking numerical advantage as performance improves.
coachingPoints: Advance the entire team, not only the football.
Maintain connection between defensive, midfield and forward lines.

Preserve width while remaining connected.
Maintain protection behind possession.
React immediately if the football is turned over.

Whether the defensive line advances.
Whether gaps form between playing lines.

successIndicators: Provide options ahead and behind possession.

Half-back connection structures.
Wing progressions.
Deep switches.
High-wing inboard connections.

Forward-half switches.

Whether all three lines remain connected.
Whether players reorganise after changes of direction.
Whether turnover protection and transition response are effective.
progressions: Add scoreboard and time-critical match scenarios.

Remove all reference markings and coach prompts.

Retain wing and central reference channels.
Limit each block to one starting situation.
Pause between phases for structural feedback.
successIndicators: Exit the defensive half with control.
Maintain width, depth and rear support.
Connect defensive, midfield and forward lines.
Switch possession while advancing the team.
Use wing and central options appropriately.
Vary disposal length and attacking tempo.

Maintain connection through repeated direction changes.

title: Defensive Line Manipulation
primarySkill: Manipulating a defensive line before attacking through it.
objective: Develop players’ ability to move, stretch and disorganise a defensive line before selecting the most effective attacking lane.
groundSize: A 65-metre-long by 50-metre-wide area divided into a possession zone, defensive line and attacking zone.
setup:
Use ten attackers against seven defenders.
Position four defenders across a marked defensive line.
Position three additional defenders behind the line.
Begin the football in the possession zone.
Place attackers across both outside channels, the corridor and behind possession.
Mark three attacking gates beyond the defensive line.
Defenders may slide laterally but may not cross the line until the football does during introductory repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with controlled possession in front of the defensive line.
Attackers use short disposals, switches, decoy leads and positional rotations to move defenders.
Defenders slide and communicate to protect the three attacking gates.
The attacking team may not enter through a gate until it has created a clear numerical or spatial advantage.

Supporting attackers accelerate ahead, beside and behind the receiver.

Attackers score one point for breaking the line.

Defenders score two points for intercepting or forcing a rushed entry.
Reset with the defenders changing their starting alignment.
Rotate defensive-line roles after three possessions.
coachingPoints: Move defenders before attempting to penetrate.
Use width to stretch the line.
Use decoy movement to occupy central defenders.
Change disposal speed once the defensive line becomes unstable.
Avoid passing repeatedly without altering defender positioning.
Maintain support behind possession during the manipulation phase.
Attack decisively when the gap appears.
Continue movement after the line is broken.

Whether possession changes defender positioning.
Whether wide and central attackers maintain useful separation.

Increase the width of the area.
Pause to identify defensive movement after each disposal.

title: Decoy Switch and Re-Entry
primarySkill: Using an apparent switch to open a return attacking lane.
objective: Teach players to initiate a switch, draw defenders across and then re-enter through the space opened behind the shifting defensive structure.
groundSize: A 60-metre-long by 55-metre-wide area divided into left, central and right channels.
setup:
Use nine attackers against seven defenders.
Begin possession in one outside channel.
Position attackers behind the football to support an apparent switch.
Position one or two attackers in central holding roles.
Defenders begin compressed towards the starting side.
Mark a scoring gate in the original-side corridor and another on the far side.
Attackers may use either gate.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession near one outside channel.
Rear support initiates a switch towards the opposite side.
Defenders shift across to protect the apparent destination.
Central holding players monitor the space opening behind the defensive movement.
Before the switch is completed, the ball carrier may return possession through a central connector.
An original-side attacker leads into the vacated corridor.
The football is delivered back through the opened lane.
Attackers score two points for a successful re-entry through the original-side gate.
They score one point for completing the full switch and progressing through the far gate.
Defenders score two points for intercepting the re-entry.
The attacking team must decide whether the re-entry is genuinely available.
Restart from the opposite side.
coachingPoints: Sell the switch through body position and supporting movement.
Central players must hold rather than follow the transfer.
Scan behind the shifting defenders.
Re-enter only when the original-side lane has genuinely opened.
Avoid turning back into pressure if defenders remain balanced.
Original-side runners should delay their movement.
Deliver the football to the receiver’s forward side.
Complete the full switch when the defence does not overcommit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the switch movement influences defenders.
Whether central players retain useful positions.
Whether original-side runners delay correctly.
Whether the ball carrier scans before re-entering.
Whether players force the deceptive option.
Whether the full switch remains available.
progressions: Allow defenders to disguise their level of commitment.
Continue through to a forward entry and score.
regressions: Tell attackers when the defence will overcommit.
Pause when the switch reaches the middle of the ground.
successIndicators: Re-enter through the opened lane when appropriate.
Complete the full switch when the deceptive option is unavailable.

howTheDrillWorks:
Attackers compete to secure possession inside the central zone.
The attacking team uses short disposals and movement to draw defenders towards the football.
One attacker deliberately holds away from the immediate possession.
The roaming defender chooses whether to enter the central zone or cover an outside receiver.
Once a defender commits, attackers identify the free player.
Possession is released either to the free central attacker or an outside receiver.
The receiver accelerates towards the scoring gate.
Central attackers spread and provide the next support.

They score a second point for progressing through a scoring gate.
Defenders score two points for a turnover or forced stoppage.
Rotate the holding attacker and roaming defender.

title: Tempo Trap Escape

setup:

Position three attacking runners beyond the pressing line.
Position two defenders in the escape zone.

Defenders gradually press forward and reduce space.
Attackers retain possession while monitoring the space behind the pressing line.
Forward runners adjust their depth and movement.
When defenders overcommit, the ball carrier or supporting player accelerates the attack.
Possession is moved through or over the pressing line.
Forward runners connect with the escaping possession.
Attackers score two points for breaking the press and reaching the final gate.
They score one point for retaining possession for ten disposals without an escape.
Defenders score two points for forcing a turnover in the possession zone.
The defending team may vary when and how aggressively it presses.
Rotate forward runners and pressing defenders.
coachingPoints: Control possession without becoming passive.
Scan behind the pressing line before receiving.
Draw defenders forward through secure short disposal.
Forward runners should remain connected without coming too close.
Change tempo collectively once the trap is ready to break.
The first escape disposal must be clean.
Support runners should accelerate immediately.
Do not attempt the escape before sufficient space exists.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers recognise the pressing behaviour.
Whether possession draws defenders forward.
Whether players scan the space behind the press.

title: Forward-Line Rotation Against Zone
primarySkill: Rotating forward roles to disrupt a zonal defence.
objective: Develop coordinated forward rotation that moves zonal defenders, opens scoring space and provides varied forward-entry targets.
groundSize: The attacking half of the ground using full width.
setup:
Use nine attackers against eight defenders.
Organise defenders in a zonal structure across the forward half.
Position attackers in deep-forward, high-forward, pocket and midfield-connection roles.
Begin possession 60–75 metres from goal.
Use normal goals.
Mark optional forward reference zones for the first repetitions.
Defenders may pass attackers between zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession outside 50.
Deep and high forwards begin coordinated rotations.
One forward leads to occupy the nearest zone defender.
Another forward clears through to move a second defender.
A third attacker replaces the vacated scoring space.
Midfield and high-forward players maintain possession until a clear entry appears.
The ball carrier selects the best available option.
Play continues until a score, turnover or defensive exit.
One bonus point is awarded when rotation creates an uncontested mark or controlled shot.
Defenders score two points for an intercept and clean exit.
Reset with defenders changing their zonal alignment.
Rotate attacking roles after three possessions.
coachingPoints: Move defenders before entering the forward line.
Rotate through high, deep and lateral positions.
Do not allow all forwards to lead towards the football.
A clearing run must create space for another attacker.
Maintain at least one deep scoring threat.
High forwards should remain connected to possession.

Apply immediate pressure after a turnover.

Begin possession in a varied field position.

Repeat with different scores, times and starting positions.
howTheDrillWorks:

If a clear scoring opportunity appears, the attacking team may take it.
Turnovers are played live.
Normal match scoring applies.
The leading team wins if it remains ahead when the clock expires.
The defending team wins if it takes the lead.
Coaches reset the score and time after each scenario.
Rotate leadership and on-field communication responsibilities.

Retain possession without becoming motionless.
Maintain support behind the football.
Use safe width and boundary positions when appropriate.

Communicate time, score and field position.

Use normal goals.

title: Risk-Reward Corridor Game
primarySkill: Balancing corridor reward against turnover risk.

Divide players into two balanced teams.

howTheDrillWorks:

Players assess the defensive structure.

Restart with a different defensive structure.

High reward does not justify a low-percentage disposal.
